Always declare arthritis on travel insurance. Pack double the medication, split between hand and hold luggage. During travel, request assistance, stand and stretch frequently, and consider accessible destinations. Planning, pacing, and permission to rest are key for a comfortable journey.

Travelling with Arthritis: Your Complete UK Guide

Arthritis should never stop you from exploring the world. With smart planning and a few adjustments, you can enjoy holidays that leave you with memories — not flare-ups.

Before You Go

Talk to your GP or rheumatologist at least 6 weeks before departure. They can:

  • Provide a medical letter for carrying medications through airport security
  • Adjust your medication schedule for time zone changes
  • Recommend travel-friendly pain relief options

Insurance is essential. Always declare arthritis on your travel insurance — failing to do so could void your cover. Specialist providers like AllClear and Free Spirit cover pre-existing conditions at reasonable rates.

Packing Smart

  • Medication: Pack double what you need, split between hand luggage and hold luggage
  • Compression socks: Reduce swelling on long flights or drives
  • Heat/cold packs: Reusable gel packs are permitted in hold luggage
  • Supportive shoes: Break them in before you travel
  • Lightweight luggage: Choose bags with four spinner wheels and telescopic handles

During the Journey

Flying: Request an aisle seat for extra legroom and the ability to stretch. Most airlines offer priority boarding and wheelchair assistance — book these in advance through Special Assistance. Stand and move every 30–45 minutes.

Driving: Stop every 90 minutes to stretch. Use cruise control where possible to reduce ankle strain. Heated seats can help stiff backs and hips.

Train travel: UK rail companies offer the Disabled Persons Railcard (£20/year), saving you a third on most fares. Book assistance through Passenger Assist at least 24 hours ahead.

Accessible UK Destinations

  • The Cotswolds: Many accessible cottages with level-access showers and hot tubs
  • Lake District: Accessible boat trips on Windermere; Brockhole visitor centre has excellent facilities
  • Cornwall: The Eden Project offers mobility scooter hire and step-free access
  • Edinburgh: Many hotels near the Royal Mile with lift access; hop-on buses reduce walking

Abroad: Top Tips

  • Mediterranean climates (Spain, Portugal, Greece) are popular with arthritis patients — warmth eases stiffness
  • All-inclusive resorts reduce the stress of planning and walking between restaurants
  • Cruise holidays let you unpack once while visiting multiple destinations, and ships have excellent accessibility

Managing Flare-Ups Away from Home

Pack a "flare-up kit": topical anti-inflammatory gel (e.g., Voltarol), paracetamol, a cold compress, and a list of local pharmacies. The European Health Insurance Card (EHIC) or its replacement, the UK Global Health Insurance Card (GHIC), covers emergency treatment in EU countries.

Key Takeaway

The secret to arthritis-friendly travel is planning, pacing, and permission to rest. Choose destinations with good accessibility, pack thoughtfully, and don't be afraid to ask for help.

Practical next steps for Travelling with Arthritis: A UK Guide to Pain-Free Holidays

If you came here about Travelling with Arthritis: A UK Guide to Pain-Free Holidays, pick one change you can keep for a fortnight rather than overhauling everything at once. Note what hurts, what helps, and what you have already tried, then take that list to your GP, rheumatology nurse or physiotherapist so the conversation stays concrete.

In many areas you can ask community musculoskeletal services about self-referral to physiotherapy or lifestyle support without waiting for a hospital letter. Check your GP surgery website or the NHS App for the route that applies where you live.

Making information usable

Treat articles like this as a starting map, not a personal care plan. Highlight one idea to try for two weeks, then review. If symptoms are new, rapidly worsening, or affecting several joints with fever or unexplained weight loss, contact your GP promptly rather than waiting on self-help alone.

Reliable UK sources

Cross-check major decisions with NHS.uk, your clinical team, and NICE guidance summaries where relevant. Be wary of social posts that promise reversal of arthritis or attack standard medicines without evidence.

Building a joint-friendly routine

Start with short sessions you can repeat on most days. Warm water, cycling, or paced walking often suits stiff joints better than sudden high-impact bursts. Increase time or resistance slowly, and leave a rest day when a joint is hot, swollen or unusually painful. If you are unsure where to begin, ask about NHS physiotherapy or an exercise referral scheme via your GP surgery.

Quick questions about Travelling with Arthritis Guide

Is this a substitute for seeing a clinician? No. Use it to prepare questions and understand options, then confirm decisions with your NHS team.

How long before I judge whether a change helped? Give most habit or exercise changes at least two to four weeks, unless pain or swelling clearly worsens — in that case scale back sooner.

What should I track? Joint pain (0–10), morning stiffness time, sleep quality, and how far you can walk or how long you can type or stand. Patterns beat one-off ratings.

Safety and when to get urgent help

This page is general information for people in the United Kingdom, not personal medical advice. Seek urgent help via NHS 111 or A&E if you have sudden inability to move a joint, hot swollen joint with fever, chest pain, severe shortness of breath, or symptoms that feel immediately dangerous.
